pension-calculator.quickAnswer: Your corpus grows from today's savings plus monthly contributions, compounded to retirement age; the monthly pension is the annuity that corpus can pay over your payout years. Example: at 30 with 500,000 saved and 20,000 per month at 10% return, retiring at 60 builds a corpus of about 53,934,460, which pays roughly 520,479 per month for 20 years. Of that corpus, 46,234,460 is pure growth.
keyFacts: A pension corpus has two engines: what you contribute and how long compounding works on it.
Starting 10 years earlier can matter more than saving 50% more each month.
Monthly pension = annuity payment the corpus sustains over your chosen payout years.
Inflation shrinks future purchasing power: plan in today's money too, not just future money.
A common rule of thumb is needing 25x your annual expenses saved (the 4% rule).
Employer plans, government pensions, and personal savings stack: add them all up.
howTo: Enter your current age and the age you plan to retire.
Enter savings already set aside for retirement.
Enter how much you can contribute every month.
Enter a realistic expected annual return (7 to 10% for equity-heavy plans).
Set how many years the pension must last, and read your corpus and monthly pension.
pension-calculator.formula:
Corpus = Savings x (1 + i)^(12 x years) + Monthly x (((1 + i)^(12 x years) - 1) / i), with monthly rate i = annual return / 12.
Monthly pension = Corpus x i / (1 - (1 + i)^-n), with n = payout months.
Example: 500,000 x 1.1^30 = 8,724,700 from savings alone; 20,000 monthly at 10% for 30 years = 45,209,800; corpus = 53,934,460.
pension-calculator.workedExample:
Age 30, retire at 60, savings 500,000, monthly 20,000, return 10%, payout 20 years:
1. Years to retirement: 30.
2. Savings grow to: 500,000 x (1 + 0.10/12)^360 = 8,724,700.
3. Monthly contributions grow to: 20,000 x ((1.008333^360 - 1) / 0.008333) = 45,209,800.
4. Corpus: 8,724,700 + 45,209,800 = 53,934,460.
5. Monthly pension over 240 months at 10%: 53,934,460 x 0.008333 / (1 - 1.008333^-240) = 520,479.
6. Total contributed: 7,700,000, so growth = 46,234,460.
benefits: Translates a monthly savings habit into a concrete retirement paycheck.
Shows how much of the corpus is growth versus your own contributions.
Lets you test retiring earlier or later with one number change.
Motivates early action: watch the corpus jump when you lower your current age.
limitations: Projections are not guarantees: returns vary and are never constant.
Ignores inflation, taxes on withdrawals, and fees.
Assumes you never miss a contribution and never withdraw early.
Not retirement advice: consult a licensed financial planner for your situation.

faqs.q: How much do I need to retire?
faqs.a: A popular starting point is 25 times your annual expenses, which supports a 4% yearly withdrawal. Enter your target monthly pension here and work backward: raise the monthly contribution until the pension row matches your goal.

Match it to your asset mix. Equity-heavy portfolios have historically returned 10 to 12% long-term in India, balanced plans 8 to 9%, and conservative debt 6 to 7%. Using a lower, conservative figure keeps the plan honest.

faqs.q: Is it better to save more or start earlier?
faqs.a: Usually, starting earlier. Compounding needs time more than it needs money. A 25-year-old saving 10,000 a month often beats a 35-year-old saving 20,000 a month at the same return. Do both if you can.

faqs.q: Why does inflation matter if my corpus looks huge?
faqs.a: Because 53,934,460 in 30 years buys far less than it does today. At 6% inflation, prices roughly multiply by 5.7 over 30 years, so that corpus spends like about 9.4 million today. Always sanity-check the monthly pension against today's expenses grown by inflation.

faqs.q: What if I retire earlier than planned?
faqs.a: Two things shrink at once: fewer compounding years and fewer contributions. Try lowering the retirement age in the tool and watch the corpus fall. That gap is exactly what working a few more years buys you.

faqs.q: Should the payout return equal the growth return?
faqs.a: Ideally the payout phase uses a lower, safer return, since retirees usually shift to conservative assets. This calculator keeps one rate for simplicity, so treat the pension as slightly optimistic if you plan to de-risk after retiring.
